beats.text: Hi, I'm Vamsi, and this is Nearhand. It schedules a small business's week from plain English, and an AI agent fills the open shifts from its own team and the neighborhood.

It's Thursday morning. Chris just called out sick, and the café owner is texting around to cover his shift while serving customers. Small businesses lose sales every time that happens. Nearhand turns it into one click.

Dana runs Bean and Co. She writes this week's rules the way she'd say them: Maya off Tuesdays, a keyholder at every open and close. Muse Spark Open, Meta's open-weight model, turns them into rules she can check, and untick any it got wrong.

Then OR-Tools builds the cheapest week that follows every rule. The model talks, and the optimizer decides. It handles overtime, rest between shifts and required skills, down to the quarter hour. Four shifts are still open.
One click, and the AI agent goes to work. It's Muse Spark Open calling tools: it asks the café's own team first, then qualified people who live nearby.

Here's how it got there. It searched the neighborhood, asked the optimizer for the cheapest cover, tried giving Lucia and Omar extra hours, and skipped them because they cost more. Every number it writes is checked against the optimizer before Dana sees it. Dana approves in one click, and nothing is booked until each person says yes.

Each person gets the offer on their phone, and they can say no. Lucia can't make it, so she declines. By the time Dana is back on her planner, the agent has already offered Lucia's shift to the next best person. No group texts, no phone tag, and nobody had to chase anyone.

Bianca lives less than a mile away. Before she answers, Should I take this? gives her an honest second opinion, checked against her own calendar and her asking rate. It's on her side, not the business's. She accepts, the shift is booked, and the pay goes to someone who lives down the street.

Workers have a voice too. Sam can take the extra hours, but not all of them, so he messages the café: can I leave at three instead of five? Muse Spark Open reads that as a change request, and the code checks exactly what it means for the schedule and the cost. One click accepts it, and the agent offers the two hours Sam gave up to someone nearby.

And Chris's sick call? Dana just types it, the way she'd text it. His Thursday shift reopens, and the agent goes looking for cover, team first, then the neighborhood. A morning of texting becomes one sentence.

And it's measured, not assumed. Every model job is checked against known answers: twenty-five of twenty-five rule sets read right, the agent matching the optimizer in ten of ten test weeks, the worker's advice right twenty of twenty, and every number checked, for under three cents a plan.
Nearhand. Your week, scheduled. Your gaps, filled from down the street. Built with Muse Spark Open. Try it at nearhand dot streamlit dot app.
